rules_evaluated.rule_lead: No stale markers, no "fixed" retrospectives, no session biography.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Harm: this rule's maintainer-block extension keeps dated ATTRIBUTION but bans the JOURNEY verb. Line 85: "...then `ironies-of-automation` closes the module (moved there 2026-08-25). This file owns only what the student does." "moved there 2026-08-25" is a transition clause (verb 'moved' + bare date) narrating a completed change on a page that only DESCRIBES current lecture order — it fits the rule's own cut list ("renamed from A to B", "the registry followed on the same day") rather than its keep list (dated attribution / standing constraint / do-not-reintroduce / empirical finding). The sentence "ironies-of-automation closes the module" already states the binding fact in full; the parenthetical adds only the transition, which goes stale the next time the lecture order changes and nobody is obligated to touch this file. This is maintainer-block-only (below `<!-- maintainer -->` at line 62), not student-facing, so the harm lands on future maintainers/judges re-deriving module structure, not on a student.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Drop the parenthetical: "...then `ironies-of-automation` closes the module. This file owns only what the student does." If the move-date matters, it belongs where the lecture's OWN placement note lives (per this rule's "a removal is recorded where the beat WAS" clause), not on a page describing where it landed.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Audit closer when trimming body-prose forcing function.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Harm: rule 15's pronoun/metaphor-referent check fires on any closer, not only post-trim ones. Line 55: "...Past ten or so interventions, you have become the agent; call it and read what is there." "call it" has more than one plausible referent (name the drift? name the intervention count? call time on the run?), and "what is there" is a vague spatial stand-in for a concrete noun (the transcript / the scrollback) never named in the clause. A reader cold-reading this closer cannot point at exactly what "it" and "there" mean without inferring from context two sentences away. (Separately, the file's own Lean-intro trim did remove a bullet from Phase 1, but the remaining Phase 1 bullet has no dangling reference to it — that trim is clean.)
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Name the object: "call it and read the transcript so far" (or "...and read what the session has produced") instead of the vague "what is there."

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: A slogan that is false as stated is not punchy framing — run the truth test before reaching for §12.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Harm: line 56 ("If the run goes completely off the rails, stop it. The trace is the result either way.") asserts an absolute ("either way" = regardless of finishing or being stopped) about the file's own mechanism. The cheapest counterexample is this same file's own maintainer block, line 83: "**Capability verified:** ... Ctrl+C mid-tool-call can corrupt the `.jsonl`..." — Ctrl+C is exactly one of the two ways to "stop it" the body just named, and the maintainer's own verified caveat says that path can corrupt the very trace the body claims survives "either way". A student who hard-stops a stalled run on this claim's authority may believe the trace is intact when it may not be, which matters because M5 forks from that trace.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Soften the absolute: "Most of the time, the trace is the result either way" or fold in the caveat ("stop it cleanly if you can; a corrupted trace is data too") so the claim doesn't contradict the maintainer's own Capability-verified line.

rules_evaluated.evidence: Harm: `curriculum/vocabulary.md` line 25 states plainly "Noun-run for the agent sitting is banned in student-facing body — engineers don't say it", and line 40 gives the exact specimen: "chart callbacks say *the passage*, never 'the run'." Line 56 of this file ("If the run goes completely off the rails, stop it. The trace is the result either way.") uses "the run" as a bare noun for the agent's live unattended execution — exactly the banned shape. It fails every listed exemption: not a test/CI/eval execution, not a verbatim quote, not an artifact/path/branch name, not the "long-running" adjective form. This is M4's flagship send-off exercise, in the shared exercise library reused as the arc's canonical send-off vocabulary point, so the imprecision is not incidental — it teaches the exact word choice the training's own controlled-vocabulary registry says engineers don't use, in the one file most likely to be quoted forward.
